analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress, the president, and vice president from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: A Senate committee sent the congressional stock-trading ban to the floor calendar in December 2024, but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for members of Congress, the president, the vice president, and their spouses and young children to buy or hold individual stocks, commodities, futures, or crypto. They would have to sell those holdings within a set window, or everything could go only into broad, diversified index funds. Members who break the rules would owe fines equal to a month's salary or 10 percent of the un-divested asset each month, and the bill would also make congressional financial disclosures searchable online with a $500 fine for late trade reports. A Senate committee approved it and put it on the calendar, but the full Senate never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who currently live under conflict-of-interest rules set by people who may personally hold stock in the companies those rules affect. The bill removes the ability of the people writing laws — from drug prices to defense contracts to crypto regulation — to personally profit from those laws through their own or their family's portfolios. It would also make members' financial dealings searchable by anyone online, with real fines for hiding trades.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits covered officials from buying or holding individual stocks, commodities, futures, or digital assets; new purchases are banned immediately upon enactment and existing holdings must be sold or fully divested within 120 days of the effective date.

Allows only diversified mutual funds or ETFs, Treasury securities, and a list of specified holdings — so lawmakers can still invest broadly without betting on companies whose fate their own votes control.
Eliminates the qualified blind trust escape hatch: existing blind trusts must be emptied and dissolved, and no new ones may be maintained after 180 days past the effective date.

Imposes civil penalties of a month's salary or 10 percent of the noncompliant asset's value each 30 days a violation continues, and requires the ethics offices to publish certifications, trust documents, extensions, and penalties online.
Requires $500 fines for failing to file required trade reports under the STOCK Act, and requires financial disclosure forms to be posted online in searchable, downloadable, API-accessible formats.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the president, the vice president, and their spouses and dependent children, who would have to sell individual stocks and related investments and move the money into diversified funds; spouses with securities from their own jobs or corporate board seats are carved out. Wealth-management and trust firms would lose the blind-trust administration business this bill phases out, while members who choose to comply would bear transition costs and some tax friction on divestiture.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: The ban is delayed: the divestiture requirement applies on and after March 31, 2027, so officials' existing portfolios would remain untouched for well over two years after enactment.

The spouse carve-out is broad: a spouse's compensation from their own job or corporate board service — including stock and dividend reinvestment in that same security — is excluded, which critics could use to keep significant individual-stock exposure in the family.

Some members and good-faith observers argue the ban could deter candidates of modest means from running for office, since the fines reach a full month's salary per violation, and that a broad index-fund-only rule is one size fits all for small business owners and family farmers (the bill does include limited exceptions for those).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — lawmakers cannot personally trade on laws they write — is large and durable, and the committee-reported version strengthened it by extending coverage to the president and vice president, adding crypto, and closing the blind-trust escape hatch. The real weaknesses are timing and loopholes: a March 2027 effective date and a wide carve-out for a spouse's own-employer stock. Those flaws trim the bill's value but do not change its central effect.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Homeland Security committee approved it and placed it on the Senate's calendar of bills awaiting action, but the chamber never voted on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on April 17, 2023, joined by 23 cosponsors — all Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on.
The bill was referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, which ordered it reported favorably with a substitute amendment on July 24, 2024.

On December 19, 2024, the committee reported the bill with an amendment in the nature of a substitute (Senate Report 118-309), and it was placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 729.

The committee substitute broadened the ban: it added the president and vice president, added digital assets like crypto to the prohibited holdings, eliminated qualified blind trusts as a compliance route, and set the divestiture deadline at March 31, 2027.
The bill sat on the Senate calendar for the final two weeks of the session; the full Senate never debated or voted on it, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and their families, whose ability to hold and trade individual stocks while writing the laws that move those stocks remains unchanged. No new ban took effect for anyone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress keeping their portfolios

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban congressional stock trading and ownership and built a bloc of 23 cosponsors behind it.

for.name: Sen. Gary Peters
for.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill through markup, reported it favorably with a strengthened substitute amendment, and placed it on the Senate calendar in December 2024.

for.name: 23 Democratic and independent cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Brown, Warren, Sanders, Tester, Fetterman, and King
for.what_they_did: Signed onto the bill, giving it unanimous backing within the Senate's Democratic caucus (including one Republican-caucus independent, Sen. King).

against.name: Senate floor leadership
against.role: Majority Leader controlling the Senate calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote despite it sitting on the calendar through the final weeks of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Provided no cosponsors to the bill, leaving it entirely within the Democratic and independent caucuses.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, and no Republican signed on; the committee's favorable report and the calendar placement were under Democratic control, but the Senate as a whole never voted.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their families
industries.note: The bill would force them to sell individual stocks, crypto, and similar holdings and to dissolve blind trusts, with monthly fines of a month's pay or 10 percent of the asset for noncompliance. This is the concentrated interest the bill directly targets, and its inaction means nothing changed for them.

industries.industry: The president and vice president (and their families)
industries.note: The committee substitute extended the ownership and trading ban to the White House, closing a gap in earlier versions. Under the bill as reported they would face the same divestiture rules as members of Congress.

industries.industry: Wealth-management, brokerage, and trust administration firms
industries.note: The bill phases out qualified blind trusts, which would eliminate blind-trust administration revenue, but it steers officials' money into diversified mutual funds and ETFs, where index-fund managers would be the default home for divested portfolios.
